5209.dq: p.219 fn.144: "'Dans la plupart des langues, cette unité accentuelle est ce qu'on appelle couramment le mot' (Cf. Martinet, A., 1980, Éléments de linguistique générale, p. 89). Nous avons préféré utiliser le terme d'unité accentuelle au lieu de celui de 'mot phonologique' pour éviter de recourir à une terminologique qui pourrait interférer avec la morphologie ou la syntaxe." (p.159 §1.3.3: 'L'uni…
5209.prule: Stress (accent) is predictable and non-distinctive: it falls on the first syllable of the accentogenic element of the accentual unit, i.e. the first syllable of the radical (root/stem). Proclitic syllables cannot bear stress: the class prefix ha(n)-, a syllabic nasal, any syllable whose nucleus is schwa (e.g. the class prefix kə-), and proclitic pronouns. Hence surface stress is on the first syllable of the unit unless a proclitic precedes, in which case it is on the second. Examples (p.159): ['wɔ:mna] 'eat!', [ha'la:nte] 'man', [kə'demat] 'tongue (organ)' vs ['demat] 'tongues', [ń'kpa:s ('ma:le)] 'I cultivated rice', [(ha'la:nte) han'da:ŋ] 'a big man', [ha'bi:k 'bit.ń] 'he saw a dog'. Stress is realised as extra intensity and, to some extent, extra pitch (p.158).
5209.srule: In accentual units of more than three syllables an 'echo' accent, comparable to a secondary stress, falls on the penultimate syllable: [fń'racˌta:nde] 'flirt' (p.159: "Dans les unités accentuelles de plus de trois syllabes, on peut noter un écho d'accent assimilable à un accent secondaire... sur l'avant dernière syllabe.").
5209.quote: p.158: "La place de l'accent est prévisible. En règle générale, l'accent porte sur la première syllabe de l'unité accentuelle, sauf lorsque celle-ci est un élément proclitique. La syllabe ha(n)-, la nasale syllabique Ń et une syllabe dont la voyelle [ə] est le noyau constituent des éléments clitiques. Leur présence implique que l'accent se porte sur la deuxième syllabe." ... p.166: "La place de celui-ci n'assume aucune fonction distinctive; l'accent occupe une place déterminée dans l'unité accentuelle: il frappe la première syllabe de l'élément accentogène, en l'occurrence le radical. De ce f…
5209.loc: Tome I, Ch. I §1.3 'Phonétique supra-segmentale: l'accent', §1.3.2 'Place de l'accent' p.158 and p.159 (restatement, examples, echo accent, §1.3.3 'Unité accentuelle', fn.104); Ch. II p.166 (radical-initial, non-distinctive); pp.168-169 (tonal hypothesis rejected); §2.5.3.1 p.219 fn.144 (accentual unit = phonological word), p.220 (max five syllables); §2.6.2 p.251 (demarcative function). page numbers are in the page header; the on-file locator's pp. 159-160/167/252 are these same passages numbered one page too high.
5209.idn: Mbodj describes balante so:fa, which he presents as a component of the kənto:he (Kantohe) dialect, 'celui des Balantes dont le territoire est entièrement situé dans la partie nord de la Guinée-Bissau'; §0.2.2 (p.15) divides kənto:he into two sub-dialects, so:fa and fac. His field surveys were in the Oio and Cacheu regions, with informants from those regions living in Bissau, Canchungo, Ncan and Mbuti, and initial work with a Balanta speaker in Dakar (Intro §0.4.1, p.17). Glottolog lists Kantohe as a dialect of Balanta-Kentohe (bala1301); the variety is not Balanta-Ganja (bala1302).
5209.exq_: p.159: "Autrement dit, l'accent frappe toujours la première syllabe de l'élément accentogène ou la deuxième syllabe de l'unité accentuelle lorsque la première est une syllabe proclitique comme indiqué ci-dessus."
5209.tone: The author explicitly rejects a tonal analysis for Balanta Sofa (pp. 168-169): no tonal minimal pairs were found, the H/L word melodies expected under a two-tone hypothesis do not occur, and no grammatical function of tone was identified; the raised pitch on the stressed radical-initial syllable and the 'pont tonal' between intonation groups are treated as phonetic correlates of accent/intonation ('les réalisations tonales doivent être considérées comme des phénomènes phonétiques'). Only primary accent is marked in phonetic transcriptions. NB the sister language Balanta-Ganja (bala1302) is analysed as tonal (H vs L) by Creissels 2024 / Creissels & Biaye 2016; that is a different language under Glottolog and a different author's analysis, not a conflict for bala1301.
5209.sec_quote: Dans les unités accentuelles de plus de trois syllabes, on peut noter un écho d'accent assimilable à un accent secondaire (que l'on pourrait indiquer par le symbole ˌ) sur l'avant dernière syllabe. Ex.: [fń'rac̚ˌta:nde] 'flirt'

5209.cfw: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 2 other works consulted do not discuss stress.

contra.head: A handbook chapter says Bhatise has interacting tones and stress accents, not the Indus Kohistani pitch accent
contra.detail: One sentence in a survey chapter on Indic dialectology, with no source given for it (the chapter's reference list has no Bateri or Indus Kohistani work; Zoller appears only for 1988 Bangani, Baart 1997 for Kalam Kohistani). It states, p. 436: 'Bhatise is on the east bank of the Indus opposite Besham. Instead of the pitch accent system of other varieties of Indus Kohistani, Bhatise has a complex system of interacting tones and stress accents.' This runs against the entry's pitch-accent classification, which rests on Zoller 2005 (pp. 22-23: B lemmata marked rising/falling but 'never checked with the speech analyzer'; B 'expected' to be like J) and against Strand's first-hand description of tw…

5210.dq: In case of the B words, many of the have been marked either with the rising or the falling accent. ... (p. 26, rule 2) Each morpheme contains one syllable either with a rising or a falling accent.
5210.prule: Lexical pitch accent (as transcribed, unanalysed): each Bateri word in the dictionary carries one accented syllable, marked rising (acute) or falling (grave), whose position varies from lexeme to lexeme (initial in áṅgo 'courtyard', àmbūr 'pliers'; final in aṅgùi 'finger', axòr 'hay', adràk 'ginger', ará 'saw'); no rule predicting the place of the accent is given. Zoller expects the B system to be 'quite similar' to the Jijali Indus Kohistani system (two contrastive accent contours, rising vs falling; 'each morpheme contains one syllable either with a rising or a falling accent'; contour contrast neutralised on short vowels in polysyllables), but states that the B rising/falling marking was never checked instrumentally.
5210.srule: None stated for Bateri. (For J compounds Zoller marks a dominant nucleus accent with the other accent at a lower level, p. 28; not stated for B.)
5210.quote: The lemmata from B and G have not been analyzed in this way. This means the following: in the majority of cases, accent marking of the G words only indicates the place of the accent. ... In case of the B words, many of the [sic] have been marked either with the rising or the falling accent. This marking, however, was never checked with the speech analyzer. However, since B and G appear to have similar cases of accent shift under specific conditions (a synopsis of the rules for J is given below in section 2.3.), it is to be expected that the accent systems of B and G are quite similar to those…
5210.loc: Ch. 2 'Technical aspects of the dictionary', sec. 2 'On phonology and tonology', pp. 22-23; sec. 3 'Some pitch accent rules', p. 26 rules 1-2; Ch. 1 sec. 1.5 'Own research', pp. 6-7 (B and G accent systems: 'It was not possible to analyze their accent systems with the speech analyzer'); identity p. 1 and abbreviation list p. 41 'B = Bhat.ise (also called Bat.er.a)'; '(B)'-tagged lemmata passim.
5210.tone: Zoller treats Bateri (B) as having a pitch accent system of the Indus Kohistani/Shina kind: one accented syllable per morpheme/word with a rising vs falling contour contrast; B differs tonetically from J by a shorter peak-delay, so the accent mark is often written on the consonant preceding the tone-bearing vowel (p. 23, p. 26 rule 1). He states explicitly that the B accent system 'was never checked with the speech analyzer' and that only J 'has been completely phonologized and tonologized' (p. 22); the similarity to J is his expectation ('it is to be expected'), not a demonstrated result. No word-stress rule separate from the accent is described.

However, since B and G appear to have similar cases of accent shift under specific conditions ... it is to be expected that the accent systems of B and G are quite similar to those of J. ... The existence of many minimal pairs proves that Indus Kohistani has two pitch accents, one rising and the other falling. ... 2. Each morpheme contains one syllable either with a rising or a falling accent.

5211.caution: This reading rests on a search-engine excerpt of the source, not the full page.
5211.dq: III. The most noteworthy difference in accent exists among words of two syllables, some having an even stress on both syllables, and some having a real accent on the first. (p. 15; word accent; the 'stress' of pp. 54 and 145 is sentence emphasis on an object / a statement, treated in the syntax)
5211.prule: No Bviri-specific accent placement rule beyond remark V. Santandrea 1961 treats Ndogo, Sere, Tagbu, Bai and Bviri together; sec. 4 'Accent' gives, 'especially of Ndogo', 'suggestions (I shall not call them rules)': I. monosyllables unproblematic; II. 'a good few' polysyllables are compounds of monosyllables, 'each one of which must have its own accent duly stressed' ('denje SPEAK, vvindii REPAIR, tokponje QUARREL, kuri); III. disyllables have either 'an even stress on both syllables' or 'a real accent on the first', the latter being words with l, r, n in the second syllable (toro, kátá, mele, ngele, kele, téné, sènè, koro, moro), and where « r » is concerned the second syllable is often lost (mbòro = mbòò, kóró = kóó); IV. reduplicated disyllables accent syllables 1 and 3; p. 29: 'the accent usually lies on the first syllable of dissyllables'. Remark V extends this to Bviri: 'Most of the remarks made for Ndogo hold good', adding only that Bviri often drops a final vowel (esp. -i after n) in compounds (kon(i), son(i) - kuukon, sonson) and in words of [foreign] origin (del(i) GOAT, uton(i) HYENA). The language is tonal (sec. 5 'Tone', pp. 16-33; Wáũ 2020: three level tones).
5211.srule: None stated as such. In compounds each monosyllabic component 'must have its own accent duly stressed'; in reduplicated disyllables 'accents lie on the first and third syllables' (p. 29; lebelebe, reperepe, kacakaca), exception mbulambula with the accent on the second syllable (p. 15 IV b).

The following suggestions (I shall not call them rules) may serve as a guide for Ndogo. ... III. The most noteworthy difference in accent exists among words of two syllables, some having an even stress on both syllables, and some having a real accent on the first. ... V. Bviri. Most of the remarks made for Ndogo hold good. Moreover note the following: (a) the final vowel of such words as those spoken of in III., especially if that be « i » and the conso…

Bviri', running onto p. 16); sec. 5 'TONE', p. 17 (levels) and p. 29 point (d); p. 26 (accent on doubled vowel). Read from Google Books search-within-volume excerpt of vol. (b) occasionally the opposite phenomenon is met with, viz. the accent lies on the second syllable, though it cont…
5211.tone: Tone is the word-prosodic system. Santandrea 1961 sec. 5 'TONE' occupies pp. 16-33: p. 17 '... above (low, mid, high, very high) may well represent, as already hinted...'; p. 29 'reduplication is as a rule « sameness » of tones throughout the whole word'; pp. 25/28 higher tone on the first component in 'i' + reduplication. Wáũ 2020 p. 24 (open text, consulted again): 'In Viri, there are three tone levels, namely, high (H), low (L) and mid (M). The mid tone in Viri is often left unmarked.... Viri tone has both grammatical and lexical functions.' Bilal 2004 (OPSL 9: 180) likewise three level tones, lexical and grammatical. Neither modern source mentions stress or accent; Santandrea's accent remarks are offered as pronunciation 'suggestions', not rules.

tn.quote: Since all tones occur at one of three levels, Viri is classified as a register tone language. If a contour tone occurs in a word it is composed of two different tones, and there are also two vowels. In Viri, there are three tone levels, namely, high (H), low (L) and mid (M). The mid tone in Viri is often left unmarked. ... This illustrates that Viri tone has both grammatical and lexical functions.
tn.cite: Wáũ, Clement Mur'bá. 2020. The Structure of the Noun Phrase in Viri. SIL Electronic Working Papers 2020-002. Dallas: SIL International (sec. 3.3 Tone system, pp. 24-26); cross-checked Bilal, Clement Murba Wau. 2004. The Adamawa-Ubangi languages in Sudan. OPSL 9: 175-183, sec. 3 p. 180, p. 182
tn.note: Three level tones H, M, L, lexical and grammatical (e.g. ká 'is' vs kà 'was'); surface contours are two tones on two vowels; Bilal 2004 agrees; nothing on stress; Santandrea 1961 unobtainable in full.

5212.dq: An acute accent appears in only four items (7, 9 = 18, 10, and 29 = 30). This suggests that whatever it may represent, it was not systematically marked.
5212.quote: We thus assume that the phonetic values of the consonants and vowels in his representation of Carabayo correspond to those of Spanish graphemes and the Carabayo material was transliterated to IPA symbols accordingly. ... An acute accent appears in only four items (7, 9 = 18, 10, and 29 = 30). This suggests that whatever it may represent, it was not systematically marked. Therefore we disregard it for establishing hypothetical phoneme inventory. [Table 1, p. 3: 7 ɲa-nauué ‘give me, show me’; 9 agó ‘bring’; 10 amá ‘come’; 18 pinə-gó ‘bring shrimp/prawn’; 29 ané ui konə; 30 ané uikarə]
5212.loc: p. 2, 'Materials and Methods', second paragraph (transliteration of Juan Berchmans de Felanix's 1969 wordlist); Table 1 'All attested linguistic material for Carabayo', p. 3, items 7, 9, 10, 18, 29, 30.
5212.idn: Carabayo (ISO 639-3 cby), the language of an uncontacted group of the upper Río Puré / Río Bernardo area between the Putumayo and Caquetá, Colombian Amazon; the data are c. 50 words recorded from one captured family at La Pedrera in 1969.
5212.tone: The paper describes no tone, stress or accent for Carabayo; the only prosodic remark is that the missionary's acute accent (four items) is unsystematic and is set aside. Comparison with (tonal) Tikuna and 19th-c. Yurí is segmental/lexical only.

In Jebero, primary stress falls on the first syllable of disyllabic words and on the second syllable of words of three or more syllables; certain suffixes cause modifications (Bendor-Samuel 1981: 35-36, 73-74; Wise 1999: 313; Valenzuela & Gussenhoven ms.). 5213.dq: Finalmente, el acento no es fonológico en cahuapana. (Valenzuela 2011: 278) — no source specifies the domain of Shawi stress.
5213.prule: None stated in any reachable source. Valenzuela 2011: 278 says stress is not phonological (non-contrastive) in Cahuapanan ('las lenguas cahuapana' = Jebero and Chayahuita) but gives a placement rule only for Jebero. Rojas-Berscia, Napurí & Wang 2020 (and the identical sketch in Rojas-Berscia 2019 §3.4, whose §3.1.1 p. 44 promises 'a special focus on... the stress typology of the language') mark primary stress [ˈ] on every keyword but have no stress section: marked stress is initial in most disyllables and some trisyllables (ˈna.ni 'already', ˈta.ʃiʔ 'night', ˈsa.na.pi 'woman', ˈnaʔ.pi.ɾin 'hide', ˈnan.pi.ɾin 'live'), second-syllable in others (na.ˈɾi 'joke', na.ˈtɘʔ 'tooth', ni.ˈto.ton 'intelligent', kan.ˈpi.ta 2PL, a.ˈma.ʃa 'a bit', wa.ˈɾan.ka 'thousand', iʔ.ˈwa.ɾa 'yesterday'), and long words in the recorded passage carry several marks (ˈi.ɾa.ka.ˈma.jo, ˈpiʔ.i.ˈpi.pi.ɾin.ˈkɘ.ɾan, ˈka.to.ˈɾo.sa.ˈkɘ.ɾan); footnote 5 defers to a 'section on metrical stress' that the published article does not contain. No syllable-count rule can be read off the source without doing our own analysis.
5213.srule: Not stated (multiple [ˈ] marks per long word in the JIPA passage transcription, unexplained).

tn.translation: 1. Phonemes. In Chayahuita there are 11 consonants, 4 vowels and 4 co-vowels. … Co-vowels: length, aspiration, glottalization, nasalization. … The vowels vary etically [non-contrastively] in relative pitch: /i/ is the highest, /a/ the lowest, and the others are intermediate. … Since the pitch variation of the vowels is relative, in the clusters there are perceptible glides, but they are etic. … The cluster /ai/ has a rising glide, and /ia/ a falling one.

5214.dq: A further difference is that for some words, Kumalu, Mumengtein, and Pelenkwa have a different stress pattern, so that not only does the initial syllable have a full vowel, but it also receives stress.
5214.prule: None stated for Dambi. The survey's only stress sentence characterises Patep (initial unstressed syllables always have schwa) and names Kumalu, Mumengtein and Pelenkwa as having, for some words, a different pattern in which a full-vowelled initial syllable is stressed; Dambi is not named and no rule is given for it. Appendix B (pp. 16-27) marks stress with ' on the Dambi (Zoo village) citation forms without comment, and the marks fall on different syllables: second-syllable stress in nə'lu 'nose', ɓa'mbo 'stomach', la'ndag 'stone', ka'ndaŋk 'big', nə'ɓu 'tooth', nə'ma 'hand', ɓa'ga 'foot', ndɛ'nduk 'moon', ɓə'linek 'star', ɓə'wɛɓ 'ashes'; initial stress in 'mɛnik 'bird', 'mao 'man', 'nɔu 'dog', 'ninya 'ear', 'ŋgais 'tongue'; two marks in 'nina'ɓi 'skin' and 'lu ka'nsɛk 'head'. No placement rule can be stated from the source without our own analysis of the list.
5214.quote: There seems to be a closer correspondence of vowels between Patep and Kumalu-Dambi-Mumengtein, even though they don't share as many cognates overall. 5215.dq: While there has been no systematic study of stress in the Kru group as a whole (an exception to this is Innes's (1966) and Luckau's (1975) studies of Grebo stress where it is claimed that stress in Grebo is contrastive), there is a parallel between loss of stress in Neo-Melenesian and the shift from independent word to verbal suffix in Kru.
5215.prule: No word-stress rule stated for Dewoin in any reachable source. Marchese (1986), a comparative Kru grammar whose sample includes first-hand Dewoin data (Welmers and Mortvedt's materials plus her own consultant Bai Boikai of John Town, Bomi), states family-wide that every Kru language has three or four register tones with lexical and grammatical function; her Dewoin examples are tone-marked and Dewoin 'presumptive' pronouns are distinguished by a lengthened low-tone vowel (p. 54). On stress she states that no systematic study exists for Kru as a whole, the only exception being Grebo (Innes 1966, Luckau 1975: contrastive stress).

[p. 54] in examining the Dewoin verbal system, we note that there is a set of pronouns which Welmers (1977b) describes as "presumptive." 5217.dq: Syllable stress of individual words does not effect the intonation, but the sentence stress over rides both word stress and normal intonation contour. Sentence stress or point of emphasis is always carried by a high pitch.
5217.heavy: Syllables whose nucleus is the low vowel /a/: 'Stress is sometimes related to and predictable by the low vowel /a/'. No statement that /a/ is longer; length is said to follow stress, not to attract it.
5217.dflt: Second syllable in words of more than one syllable ('usually falls on the second syllable'); the source does not explicitly frame this as the no-/a/ case, only as the usual position.
5217.prule: Word stress is non-phonemic (not contrastive). In words of more than one syllable it usually falls on the second syllable; it is sometimes instead related to and predictable by the presence of the low vowel /a/ (i.e. a syllable with /a/ can carry the stress). Non-contrastive vowel length accompanies the stressed syllable. No lexical tone; pitch functions only as intonation, and sentence stress (high pitch) overrides word stress.

5219.dq: Phonétiquement, la voyelle de toute syllabe pré-finale se réalise semi-longue en hunde. (Mateene does not say whether 'pré-finale' is counted in the word or the utterance; his examples are isolation words. Bastin 2003:504 locates the Hunde penultimate length 'at the end of an utterance or elicitation forms'. No stress of any domain is described, hence UNSTATED for stress.)
5219.prule: No word stress is stated. Hunde is described as a tone language: the Proto-Bantu tones are maintained (H written with an acute, L unmarked; where Greenberg reconstructs H on both syllables of a disyllabic stem, Hunde has H on the first syllable only: n-góko 'poule', mu-kâtsi 'femelle', -kûlu 'âgé', i-ânika, i-hûmula), while the phonological value of vowel quantity is lost; the only non-tonal prominence mentioned is phonetic: the vowel of every pre-final (penultimate) syllable is realized half-long. An independent handbook statement agrees: Bastin 2003:504 (The Bantu Languages ch. 25 §2.1) says that in Hunde 'length is limited to the penultimate vowel at the end of an utterance or elicitation forms: Hunde ìbàlé…; ìbă:lè stone'.
5219.srule: Not applicable; the source describes no secondary or non-tonal prominence other than penultimate half-length.

5219.tone: Mateene 1967 (native-speaker linguist) treats tone as the only distinctive suprasegmental of Hunde (p. 67: PB tones maintained, vowel quantity no longer phonological; §3.2 p. 70: tone correspondences, PB *HH > H on first syllable only) and never uses 'accent' or stress for Hunde; the sole prominence remark is §3.1 'la voyelle de toute syllabe pré-finale se réalise semi-longue' (phonetic penultimate half-lengthening). 5224.heavy: not applicable (the root syllable is called 'heavy' and prefixes 'light', but stress is assigned by root vs prefix status, not by a weight computation)
5224.prule: Stress is predictable from morphological structure: only root syllables bear stress; the one or two reduced-vowel prefix syllables (lexical and productive prefixes alike) never do, so the word/foot is iambic or anapestic (prefix(es) + stressed root); suffixes that are not stems in their own right are unstressed and often absorbed into the stressed root syllable. Stated for 'Tangkhul languages' as a group from the author's own Standard Tangkhul (Ukhrul), Kachai and Huishu data; Khangoi is placed in the group by classification (p. 5, Fig. 3 'Southern' branch) and its McCulloch 1859 forms are retranscribed with the prefixal vowel symbol @ (e.g. k@na 'ear', k@tha 'new', P@mit, ch@t-lo 'weep'), but no Khangoi-specific stress observation exists in any source.
5224.quote: [pp. 11-12] In Tangkhul languages, stress is always predictable. Only roots bear stress, and prefixes never bear stress. The preferred stress pattern, for a word (and foot), is iambic or anapestic. That is to say, a stem usually consists of a stressed (heavy syllable) root and one or two unstressed (light syllable) prefixes. Suffixes that are not a stem in their own right are not stressed, but these often form part of the same stressed syllable as the root. ... 5227.dq: Rensch (1978) uses the term "stressed syllable" to refer to Full syllables. That term is appropriate in that Restricted syllables typically have lower intensity than Full syllables and vowel quality and tone contours are generally not carefully controlled. (p. 10; Full vs Restricted is a word-internal stem-vs-affix distinction; sentence-level focus is treated separately on p. 17.)
5227.prule: Stress falls on the stem syllable (Mugele's 'Full' syllable = Rensch's 1978 'stressed syllable'). Affixes, clitics and grammatical particles are Restricted (unstressed) syllables with reduced inventories; tense/aspect prefixes precede the stem and person/number suffixes/clitics follow it (e.g. r+ hwa:n -na 'I'll tell you', stem stressed, suffix unstressed), so the stressed syllable is located by morphology, not by counting from an edge. Stems are almost all monosyllabic; in the rare disyllabic stems the final stem syllable is the Full (stressed) one.
5227.srule: None described. Mugele (pp. 10-11, quoting Merrifield 1963:15) notes the ballistic/controlled contrast could alternatively have been called primary vs secondary stress but treats it as a syllable-type feature of stressed syllables, not a stress degree.

5230.tone: Syllable-tone system. Norman 1971: 'A Kienyang syllable contains at the minimum a vowel (V) and a tone (T)'; eight tones (numbered 1-3, 5-9; the yang-shang category 4 is lost) that 'differ in pitch, length and contour'; 'This dialect has no tone sandhi'; nothing corresponding to Cantonese changed tones. The only toneless category is a small set of 'atonic' syllables written with a leading period (sentence particles.ba.mɔ.lɔ/.lau.ni/.ne.a; some second syllables in the Kienow comparative lexicon). Shen 2016 (HKUST PhD on the same dialect) agrees: 'Jianyang has 8 tones for monosyllabic words, and almost 8*8=64 types of combination for disyllabic words. Thus, it is natural to assume that the tone-bearing unit (TBU) of Northern Min is the syllable rather than the word' (pp. 24-25), and classes it with Mandarin/Cantonese as a syllable-tone language (Table 2.9); the word 'stress' occurs in Shen 2016 only in summaries of Roengpitya 2007 (p. 44) and Pierrehumbert 2000 (p. 97), neither about Jianyang. Shen 2012 (Shibei) and Wang 2020 (Jian'ou), other Min Bei points, likewise do not discuss stress and describe 9 and 6 syllable tones respectively; Wang 2020 reports disyllabic tone combinations 'basically keep the citation tones'. No source reached states or denies word stress.

5231.dq: Arnott 1965:78 apud Breedveld p. 130: 'In nearly all words of more than one syllable the salient syllable is the first'; McIntosh 1984:20 apud Breedveld p. 132: 'In nominals, [stress] generally occurs on the last non-final CVC or CVV syllable.' (word/nominal-level; Breedveld p. 131 separately distinguishes 'the word that receives the focus (phrasal stress)').
5231.heavy: McIntosh 1984:20 (as quoted): 'the last non-final CVC or CVV syllable' -- heavy = closed or long-vowelled syllable; Arnott's rule is quantity-insensitive.
5231.dflt: initial syllable (McIntosh 1984:20: 'the initial syllable of the nominal is stressed, regardless of its structure'); Arnott: initial in nearly all words anyway.
5231.prule: The two descriptions of nige1253 dialects, reachable only as verbatim quotations in Breedveld 1995 sec. 4.6.1, state incompatible rules. (i) Arnott 1965:78, Gombe: in nearly all words of more than one syllable the salient (stressed) syllable is the FIRST, with a few exceptions (some numerals, adverbs, question words, negative verb forms; Breedveld lists Arnott's non-initial examples cappand'e 'tens', jooweego'o 'six', teemerre 'thousand', ammaa 'but', korii 'hopefully', ndeye 'where', moye 'who', mi-noddataa 'I won't call'). (ii) McIntosh 1984:20, Kaceccereere: in nominals stress generally falls on the LAST NON-FINAL CVC or CVV syllable; if there is no such syllable the initial syllable is stressed regardless of structure (example 'kaceccere'en 'the people of Kaceccere', stress pushed back to the heavy syllable); for verbal complexes she declines to give a rule (1984:82: 'there is always one, or more than one, high-pitched syllable in the complex, which often does not sound stressed at all'). Breedveld (pp. 130-133) argues that Arnott (and Noye) 'wrongly equated high pitch with stress' and that the weight rule is correct: e.g. rawaandu 'dog' is initial-stressed for Arnott but penult (= last non-final heavy) for Klingenheben 1963 and Breedveld. Whether the disagreement is analytical or dialectal (Gombe vs Zaria) cannot be settled without the primaries.

5232.dq: The final margin of the phonological word is characterized by potential pause. The phonological word is the level of distribution of the syllable: one syllable is stressed in each word. 5232.prule: Register tone language: three level phonemic tones (high, mid, low), the syllable is the unit of tone placement and every syllable carries exactly one tone (sec. 2.3, 5.2). Stress: the pause-bounded phonological word carries one and only one stress, which is 'neither contrastive nor used at all in connection with semantic emphasis'; its position is not stated ('the factors that condition stress have not been studied'). Examples (5) mark the single stress on either grammatical word of two-word phonological words (aca 'yat 'I have taken it', 'moc met 'give the child something', 'mony dit 'old man') and on monosyllables ('lec 'teeth'). No word-stress rule can be coded.
5232.srule: None; one stress per phonological word.

5233.loc: §2.2 'Les unités suprasegmentales: les tonèmes', pp. 76-77, with §§2.2.1-2.2.5 pp. 77-81, Résumé p. 82 and TOC p. 104
5233.idn: Nyong (Mubako / Daganyonga; Bali-Kumbat variety, NW Cameroon)
5233.tone: Tone language ('un parler à tons'): three level tonemes /´/ high, /-/ mid, /`/ low plus two contour tonemes (rising, falling), the contours analysed as unit tonemes not sequences of level tones; minimal pairs e.g. ká- 'crabe' vs kà- 'coussin', búm- 'moustique' vs bùm- 'guerre'; Résumé p. 82: 23 consonants, 8 short and 6 long vowels, 'trois tons ponctuels et deux tons modulés'. The sketch says nothing about stress/accent: TOC pp. 102-105 lists only tonemes under 2.2; Notes préliminaires (pp. 22-26) and Résumé (pp. 82-84) have no accent remark; a search for accent/stress/tonique/intensité/prominence gives no hits.

tn.quote: Le Bali-kumbat est donc un parler à tons ... Toute voyelle, centre de syllabe et toute nasale syllabique subissent un traitement prosodique. Elles sont les seules à servir de support à un ton. Dans le régistre tonal de ce parler, nous avons noté l'existence de trois tons ponctuels: haut /´/ ... moyen /-/ ... bas /`/ ... A ces trois ponctuels s'ajoutent deux tons mélodiques: montant /ˇ/ ... /ˆ/ ... Les tonèmes montant /ˇ/ et descendant /ˆ/ ne sont pas à considérer comme une sucession de deux tonèmes ponctuels
tn.translation: Bali-Kumbat is therefore a tone language ... Every vowel (syllable nucleus) and every syllabic nasal undergoes prosodic treatment. They alone serve as the support of a tone. In the tonal register of this variety we noted the existence of three level tones: high /´/ ... mid /-/ ... low /`/ ... To these three level tones are added two melodic (contour) tones: rising /ˇ/ ... [falling] /ˆ/ ... The rising and falling tonemes are not to be regarded as a succession of two level tonemes
tn.cite: Kouonang (épouse Nganmou), Alise. 1983. Esquisse phonologique du parler bali-kumbat. Mémoire de Maîtrise en Linguistique, Université de Yaoundé. 105 pp. [MPG PuRe hdl:11858/00-001M-0000-0012-7F02-1]
tn.note: Five tonemes: high, mid, low plus rising and falling, the contours treated as unit tonemes (a two-level analysis 'would split the vowel into two morae'). Mid is rarest. Nothing on stress or downstep.

5234.prule: Primary stress falls on the first syllable of every word (realised as higher pitch and loudness); fully regular, so the author omits it from transcriptions.
5234.quote: Stress is always on the first syllable of the word and is indicated by higher pitch and loudness. Since it is regular I do not write it in the phonetic transcription. The intonation drops from the first syllable towards the end of the word, except in polar questions where the intonation is falling-rising on the last syllable of the final word of the clause. Pinai-Hagahai is not a tonal language.

5235.dq: No stress system is described; the sole mention of the domain is the impressionistic 'when /u/ occurs the stress of the word was on the previous syllable, whereas when /o/ occurs, the stress was on the syllable with this vowel instead' (p. 14).
5235.prule: none stated: the only first-hand description reachable (Knobloch 2020, written from H. Liljegren's and A. Nuristani's field recordings of 1999-2017: refugee camps in Pakistan 1999-2000, Sau 2000, Jalalabad 2010, Kabul 2017) explicitly leaves stress and pitch accent unanalysed; its one stress remark is an impressionistic note that the m.sg Past Perfective ending was heard as -aalu with word stress on the preceding syllable or as -aaloo with stress on that final syllable. Examples throughout the thesis are transcribed without accent marks.
5235.quote: (p. 15) Stress and pitch accent have not been analyzed specifically in this thesis, but considering that they are phonologically relevant features in e.g. Palula (Liljegren, 2016: 72-75) and other Shina languages, they might also be of relevance for Sauji. ... (p. 14) Especially /o/ and /u/ ocurr quite often in the same places, for example the (masculine singular) Past Perfective form ending on -aalu and -aaloo. Here, a clue to this variation might be stress: when /u/ occurs the stress of the word was on the previous syllable, whereas when /o/ occurs, the stress was on the syllable with this …
5235.loc: Knobloch 2020, §4.2.3 'Phonotactics' p. 15; §4.2.2 'Vowel inventory' p. 14; §5.4 'Further research' p. 40
5235.tone: Author expects a Shina-type pitch accent may be relevant ('considering that they are phonologically relevant features in e.g. Palula (Liljegren, 2016: 72-75) and other Shina languages, they might also be of relevance for Sauji', p. 15) but did not analyse it. Liljegren 2009 (Acta Orientalia 70) p. 34 mentions 'low-rising pitch in Klk and Sw' as a possible correlate of Palula voiced aspiration; no placement statement for Sawi there either.
